questions.q: Which port is associated with SSH, encrypted remote login?
questions.explain: Port 22 is SSH. Port 23 is Telnet, its unencrypted and legacy predecessor.

questions.q: What is the key difference between POP3 (port 110) and IMAP (port 143)?
options: They are two names for the exact same protocol
POP3 downloads and often deletes mail from the server; IMAP syncs mail across devices
IMAP can only be used for sending, never retrieving, email
POP3 is encrypted and IMAP is not
questions.explain: POP3 typically pulls mail down to one device and removes it from the server, while IMAP keeps mail in sync across multiple devices.

questions.q: A firewall log shows unexpected inbound traffic on port 3389 from an external IP. What should that immediately signal to a SOC analyst?
options: SMTP — someone is sending an email
DNS — routine and safe to ignore
RDP (Remote Desktop) — a frequent entry point for ransomware
questions.explain: Port 3389 is Windows Remote Desktop Protocol; unexpected inbound RDP is one of the most common ransomware entry points in real incidents.

questions.q: Why is Telnet (port 23) considered a red flag on a modern network?
options: It was never actually a real protocol
It uses more bandwidth than any other protocol
It transmits credentials and data in plaintext with no encryption
It only works over UDP, which makes it inherently unsafe
questions.explain: Telnet sends everything, including login credentials, unencrypted — its presence alone is often the finding in a security review.

questions.q: Why do analysts treat a port number as a strong hint rather than a guarantee of what protocol is actually running?
options: Because only even-numbered ports are ever used for real traffic
Because port usage is a convention, and attackers can run other traffic, like command-and-control, over a well-known port such as 443 to blend in
Because well-known ports are not actually standardized anywhere
Because port numbers change randomly every few minutes on all networks
questions.explain: Nothing technically enforces that traffic on a given port matches that port's named protocol, which is exactly how C2 traffic hides inside normal-looking HTTPS.
